claims.text: In bcc high-entropy alloys, superconducting transition temperature is governed mainly by overall valence electron count.
Changing the overall valence electron count shifts the Fermi level relative to a peak in the electronic density of states.
Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloys have a pronounced electronic density-of-states feature close to the Fermi level.
Moving the Fermi level closer to or farther from the DOS peak changes the effective electron-phonon coupling.
A higher density of states at the Fermi level strengthens electron-phonon coupling and increases Tc.
The initial Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloy is a single-phase bcc material.
The initial Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloy has an established superconducting Tc of approximately 6-8 K.
Ti and V have similar atomic sizes but different valences.
Incrementally replacing Ti with V changes the alloy's overall electron count.
Holding phase structure and disorder comparable would isolate electron count as the principal experimental variable.
The relevant compositional range is a dirty-limit, BCS-type superconducting regime.
If increasing valence electron count moves the Fermi level toward the DOS peak, Tc should increase modestly.
Changes in Tc across the substitution series should track changes in the calculated or measured DOS near the Fermi level.
Variations in structural or compositional disorder can affect Tc in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis is restricted to compositions that remain single-phase bcc and have no significant change in structural disorder.
Failure to observe a consistent relationship among valence electron count, DOS changes, and Tc would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
